claims.text: A tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy can be engineered to exhibit a ductile-brittle-ductile transition with temperature.
Chemical complexity in the tungsten-based HEA suppresses conventional temper embrittlement.
The proposed alloy has good ductility at lower and higher temperatures but a narrow intermediate window of brittle behavior.
Conventional tungsten-based alloys normally show pronounced temper embrittlement in a narrow temperature interval.
The proposed material is a tungsten-based HEA containing several refractory elements in near-equiatomic proportions.
Controlled cooling and homogenization will produce a stable, compositionally complex microstructure in the proposed alloy.
Rapid cooling may promote embrittlement in conventional tungsten alloys.
The relevant mechanical response should be tested from room temperature to above 800 degrees Celsius.
The proposed microstructure is homogeneous and BCC.
The tungsten refractory HEA contains coherent nanoprecipitates.
Impurity segregation is suppressed in the proposed microstructure.
Coherent nanoprecipitate interfaces facilitate dislocation transmission and relieve stress concentrations.
Adding multiple refractory elements increases mixing entropy and disrupts impurity-segregation processes responsible for temper embrittlement.
The complex microstructure maintains dislocation motion at both lower and higher temperatures.
An intermediate temperature range activates a controlled and limited embrittling mechanism.
The intermediate ductility loss will be less severe than temper embrittlement in conventional alloys.
Conventional tungsten-based refractory alloys do not recover ductility at higher temperatures after temper embrittlement.
The proposed transition requires a uniform, compositionally complex microstructure, while segregation or incomplete mixing may prevent suppression of embrittlement.
Failure to observe a distinct intermediate brittle window with ductility on both sides would falsify the proposed transition.
